newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank says overnight rate too low.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank says overnight rate too low.

text.p: Central bank Governor Sheu Yuan-dong said on Tuesday Taiwan's overnight interbank lending rate was too low and said he hoped it would rise to five percent.
The rate had closed at 4.645 percent on Monday against Saturday's 4.635 close, but was up to 4.750 percent at midmorning on Tuesday when Sheu made the comment.
"The current level is too low," Sheu told reporters at the central bank. "We hope it would rise to about five percent."
Sheu said that if liquidity in Taiwan's money market were to become too lose "it could jeopardise the interests of investors".
"But right now the liquidity is at an appropriate level," Sheu added without further clarification.
Taiwan's shortest-term money rates have hovered around the five percent level for weeks, but have dipped below 4.5 percent. The overnight interbank rate closed at 4.491 percent on October 17.
Sheu said on October 7 that the level of liquidity in the Taiwan market was "slightly too loose" but that the central bank would maintain an "appropriately loose" monetary policy.
He said this meant preventing interest rates from dropping too low so as not to hurt the interest of most depositors.
Other central bank officials, including vice governor Liang Cheng-chin, have made similar statements in recent weeks.
The next meeting of the central bank board is scheduled for November 14, with the only publicly known agenda item being reform of the island's reserve system.
The last meeting on October 19 ended with no adjustment to monetary policy.

Government and central bank officials are believed to be content to leave rates roughtly where they are for fear that higher rates could choke off what recent economic indicators have shown to be the first signs of recovery after months of stagnation.
